title: Everyday American Culture – Tipping, Talking to Strangers, Work & More!

lines.text: Hello everyone. Welcome to a new episode
of Beau's Slow English. It's been
several weeks since I've posted a long
video. I've been very busy with my life
outside of YouTube and I miss it. So,
here I am.
Also, apologies if you hear my cat
meowing in the back. I had to put him in
the bedroom because he is very
talkative. Today's episode is going to
be about American culture and things you
should know if you visit the United
States or if you live here. First off,
tipping. In a lot of countries outside
of the United States, tipping is not
customary or not normal. But, in
America, there are a lot of professions
that make a lower base salary. So, what
that means is every hour that they work,
they don't make a lot of money or every
year they work, they don't make a lot of
money. So, they rely on tips to make a
living. Have you ever heard of the term
make a living? What that means is you
work to live, basically.
In the US, tipping is expected in
restaurants,
sometimes in cafes, and a lot of service
industries.
For example, I used to be a hair stylist
and my clients would give me a tip based
on the service that I provide. Tips
usually range between 15%
and 20%.
means that the service was good and 20%
means that the service was excellent.
With that said,
giving a tip on top of an already
expensive service that you're paying for
can be expensive altogether. So,
sometimes tipping does not happen and
that's okay. In restaurants, waiters and
waitresses make a pretty low base
salary. You can also tip taxi drivers
and hotel workers. Anytime I stay at a
hotel, if somebody helps me with my
luggage and suitcases, I will usually
provide them a cash tip. Cash is usually
the preferred method of payment.
However, cash is not always available.
So, sometimes people will tip on their
credit card. Warning, if you go to a
fancy restaurant, always look at the
bill. Read the entire bill. At the end,
it might show that the tip or gratuity,
which is a fancier word for tip, is
already included. So, just be careful of
that so that you are not double tipping.
Also, in the American culture, a lot of
people will make small talk with
strangers. I created a video a few weeks
ago about small talk and how to start a
conversation with a stranger so that you
sound very friendly. If I'm going to be
very honest with you, I don't like
making small talk. In fact, I don't
think anybody does because it requires a
lot of effort. You have to really think
about what questions or statements can
you make to a stranger to help them to
get comfortable around you. Most people
will probably prefer to have deeper
conversations,
which is the opposite of small talk.
Here are common topics for small talk.
Weather, sports, vacation plans, weekend
plans.
Hm, what else can you think of? It's
also normal to smile to someone and say,
"Hi, how are you?"
Hi, how are you?
Even if you don't know someone very
well. Usually, the response back is,
"I'm good. How about you?"
Or,
"I'm doing well, and you?" Because I've
worked in the customer service industry
for
practically my whole life, I have
learned the art of small talk. So, it is
a skill that you have to develop with
time.
Next topic is restaurant and food
culture. At a lot of restaurants,
especially fast food chains, they offer
free water and free soda refills.
However, you should not expect free
refills on cocktails,
a glass of wine,
anything that's not water and soda, you
pretty much have to pay for the second
cup or glass. It is true that in
America, the portion size, which is the
amount of food on your plate, is large
compared to other countries. If you do
have a large portion and you cannot
finish it in that meal, you could take
some of that food home.
You could either ask, "Could I get a
to-go box, please?"
Could I get a to-go box, please?
Or some people say doggy bag.
I have no idea why it's called doggy
bag, but that is another way to say
to-go box or
to-go container.
There are a lot of fast food restaurants
here, especially with the fast-paced
American culture. You will see fast food
chains on almost every block.
But, I think that is similar to other
very populated countries. Next topic is
the work culture and time off. In
America, if you work for a company that
is able to pay you while you're on
vacation, you're very lucky.
However, if you own your own business,
you do not get paid for the time you are
not working. Some companies will also
pay on holidays, and you don't even have
to work. It's usually major holidays,
such as 4th of July, also known as
Independence Day,
Memorial Day,
Labor Day, Christmas, and New Year's.
Oh, and of course, Thanksgiving.
Americans usually get fewer vacation
days compared to Europeans, and I hope
the American culture can copy the
European culture in that regards.
Whether you are living in the US
or coming to the US to visit, I hope
this lesson was helpful for you in
learning more about the American
culture. Thank you for watching. Please
don't forget to like and subscribe, and
feel free to share this with your
friends if you find this to be helpful
for them. See you next time. Bye.
